did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah opens the chapter with the cry “Woe!” and describes a land “beyond the rivers of Cush.” The phrase “the land of whirring wings” appears as part of the description of that land.
Did you know? Messengers are sent by sea in “vessels of papyrus”—boats made from reeds—to reach a people described as “tall and smooth-skinned” and “feared.”

Did you know? The chapter’s description of the people and the land includes the phrase “a nation of line upon line and treading down,” as well as “whose land the rivers have divided.” These expressions are repeated at the end of the chapter.

Did you know? The message in this chapter is addressed to “all you people of the world and inhabitants of the earth,” who are called to see the sign, like a banner raised on the mountains, and hear it, like the blowing of a trumpet.
Did you know? The Lord describes His position as one of quiet observation: “I will remain quiet and look from My dwelling place.” The verse also uses images of heat, light, cloud, and dew.

Did you know? The process of growth in this chapter is interrupted just as the crop is nearing ripeness: before the harvest, after the flower appears and the fruit begins to ripen, the shoots are cut off and the branches are removed.

Did you know? After the cutting, what is left becomes food for the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth; the verse says that birds of prey will spend the summer on it, and the beasts of the earth will winter on it.

Did you know? The chapter ends by describing gifts being brought to the Lord of hosts at Mount Zion. The people bringing the gifts are described with the same characteristics mentioned at the beginning of the chapter, creating a link between its opening and conclusion.
